newsitem.title: USA: Some Medicaid funds may be restored to New York.
newsitem.headline: Some Medicaid funds may be restored to New York.

text.p: The White House is studying a plan that would allow New York state to recoup half the $200 million in Medicaid funding it lost in a line-item veto this week, a U.S. official said on Wednesday.

President Clinton used the veto for the first time Monday to strike three items from balanced-budget legislation, including one giving New York preferential treatment in the funding of its Medicaid health care program for the poor.

White House aide Chris Jennings said the administration had explored a legislative solution before the bill was passed that would have restored half the $200 million to New York and was now studying whether it could do so without legislation.
"The question now remains whether we can do it on a regulatory, administrative front ourselves without legislative action," Jennings told reporters. "We think that there might be possibilities."
Clinton's decision to veto the special Medicaid provision for New York drew sharp protests from the state's politicians, including Republicans Sen. Alfonse D'Amato and Gov. George Pataki.

Under the provision Clinton vetoed, New York would have been given special dispensation to count certain health-care provider taxes with its Medicaid expenditures, boosting the amount of spending eligible for matching funds from the federal government.
Such use of taxes has been declared impermissible in other states.
The vetoed item, which was embedded in legislation that aims to eliminate the federal budget deficit by 2002, could ultimately be restored by Congress if it musters a two-thirds majority.
New York state has said it plans to challenge the veto in court.
The estimated $200 million would have been disbursed by the federal government over five years, ending in 2002.
